  // Popcount returns the number of set bits across all words of xs.
  // One OnesCount64 call per word; blocks of 16 are peeled with a recursive
  // call (no loop phis on the hot path), and the tail is dispatched by length.
  func Popcount(xs []uint64) int {
  	l := len(xs)
  	if l >= 16 {
  		return bits.OnesCount64(xs[0]) + bits.OnesCount64(xs[1]) +
  			bits.OnesCount64(xs[2]) + bits.OnesCount64(xs[3]) +
  			bits.OnesCount64(xs[4]) + bits.OnesCount64(xs[5]) +
  			bits.OnesCount64(xs[6]) + bits.OnesCount64(xs[7]) +
  			bits.OnesCount64(xs[8]) + bits.OnesCount64(xs[9]) +
  			bits.OnesCount64(xs[10]) + bits.OnesCount64(xs[11]) +
  			bits.OnesCount64(xs[12]) + bits.OnesCount64(xs[13]) +
  			bits.OnesCount64(xs[14]) + bits.OnesCount64(xs[15]) +
  			Popcount(xs[16:])
  	}
  	// At most 15 words: a binary ladder with direct returns.
  	if l >= 8 {
  		n := bits.OnesCount64(xs[0]) + bits.OnesCount64(xs[1]) +
  			bits.OnesCount64(xs[2]) + bits.OnesCount64(xs[3]) +
  			bits.OnesCount64(xs[4]) + bits.OnesCount64(xs[5]) +
  			bits.OnesCount64(xs[6]) + bits.OnesCount64(xs[7])

diff_user.system: You are optimizing a Go function. Popcount(xs []uint64) int must return the total number of set bits across all words of xs. Each candidate is scored by running it in giri, a Go SSA interpreter, on 50 test vectors. It must return the reference result on every vector, and leave xs unchanged. Among correct candidates, a lower abstract cost (the number of SSA instructions executed over all vectors) scores higher, and any correct candidate scores above any incorrect one. The only import allowed is math/bits. Keep the function's name and signature.
